# Version Control with Git and GitHub {#sec-version-control}

::: {.bookepigraph}
```{=latex}
\begin{flushright}\small
```
*Maintaining a high degree of transparency in scientific
reporting is essential not just for gaining trust and
credibility within the scientific community but also for
facilitating the development of new ideas.*

[Karthik Ram]{.smallcaps}, *Git Can Facilitate Greater
Reproducibility and Increased Transparency in Science*
(2013)
```{=latex}
\end{flushright}
```
:::

This chapter has three practical aims. By its end you will
be able to write a commit history that answers 'what
changed and why' for any analysis you run. You will be
able to build a `.gitignore` that keeps protected health
information out of a repository before the first commit
rather than after a breach. Finally, you will be able to
state exactly which single rung of the reproducibility
ladder a GitHub URL has actually earned, and which it has
not.

We begin by placing version control on the determinant
stack and naming the failure it cures. We then set out
the analyst's three judgments, the git model, and the
reading of a history, before turning to what must never
be committed. Branches, the undoing of mistakes and
merge conflicts, and remotes follow, and we close the
exposition with what git does not do. A worked example,
a note on collaborating with an LLM, and the exercises
complete the chapter.

```{r}

```

## Before you start

**Reading time.** About 60 minutes.

**Prerequisites.** @sec-crisis and @sec-levels, for the
determinant stack and the L0 rung that this chapter's
practice secures; no other chapter is assumed.
Statistically, nothing is required. R knowledge assumed:
none beyond reading a short script. The git and shell
commands that make up most of this chapter are
independent of R, and the two R chunks that appear are
read for their output, not written by the reader. Git
itself must be installed and configured; the preflight in
the setup appendix ([Git preflight](setup-appendix.qmd#sec-git-preflight)) checks both in a
few minutes.

**By the end of this chapter you will be able to
answer:**

- Can you describe the failure mode version control
  cures, the drawer of `analysis_final_v2_FINAL.R`
  files, and explain why the cure is a different kind of
  object, a history, rather than a tidier naming scheme?
- Can you explain the git model, the repository, the
  commit as an atomic, message-bearing unit, and the
  history as a tamper-evident chain, together with the
  limits of that record as evidence?
- Can you perform the everyday git operations at the
  shell, staging and committing, reading the log and the
  diff, and writing an archetype-appropriate
  `.gitignore`?
- Can you state what must never be committed in health
  research, and explain why deleting such a file in a
  later commit does not remove it from the history?
- Can you place version control on the reproducibility
  ladder, name the one rung it secures, and list the
  layers of the determinant stack it leaves exposed?

**Outline.**

- Orientation: the drawer of `FINAL` files, and the
  object that replaces it.
- Where this sits on the stack.
- The analyst's contribution: three judgments no tool
  automates.
- What version control records, and what it cures.
- The git model: repository, commit, history.
- Reading the history: the log and the diff.
- What must never be committed: `.gitignore` and PHI.
- Branches, lightly.
- Undoing things, and merge conflicts.
- The remote: GitHub, GitLab, and collaboration.
- What git does not do.
- Worked example: an untracked folder to a tagged
  repository.
- Collaborating with an LLM.
- Exercises, a cheat sheet, and further reading.
:::

## Where this sits on the stack

Version control is this book's clearest case of pure
capture at the very top of the determinant stack.
@fig-stack-version-control marks the layer it secures.
Before a repository exists, the analysis code is not
merely unpinned; it is not reliably even *locatable* by
anyone but the analyst who wrote it. Placing it under
git, and pushing it to a remote, is the single act that
lifts that top layer from nothing to L0. The input-data
layer directly beneath it is deliberately left
unhighlighted here, because this chapter's central
judgment runs the other way. Health data, unlike code,
often must be kept *out* of the very history that pins
everything else. That is the subject of the section on
`.gitignore` below.

```{r}
#| label: fig-stack-version-control
#| fig-cap: 'The determinant stack of @sec-levels, with the analysis-code layer marked as captured here. Version control is what first pins the code, lifting it from unlocatable to L0; the input-data layer immediately below is left unhighlighted on purpose, because this chapter spends as much effort keeping some data out of the history as it spends getting the code into it.'
#| fig-alt: !expr determinant_stack_alt(captures = c('Analysis code'))
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.4
plot_determinant_stack(
  captures = c('Analysis code'),
  title = 'Version control captures the analysis code; later chapters capture the rest')
```

## Orientation

If we open the folder of almost any analysis that has run
for more than a month without version control, the same
artifact greets us. There is `analysis.R`, and
beside it `analysis_v2.R`, `analysis_final.R`,
`analysis_final_v2.R`, and, inevitably,
`analysis_final_v2_FINAL.R`. A dated copy or two,
`analysis_2025-03-14.R`, sits among them, and a
`analysis_reviewer.R` from the week the referee
reports came back. Every file is a manual snapshot,
taken because the analyst feared to overwrite a
version that worked. The scheme fails in three ways at
once. It does not say which file produced the figure
in the submitted manuscript. It does not say what
differs between any two of them, so recovering a change
means reading both side by side. And it does not say
*why* any change was made, because the reason lived in
the analyst's head and is now gone.

This is the failure that version control exists to
cure. What, then, is the cure? A tidier naming scheme will
not do; the cure is a different object. A version-control
system keeps a single working copy of each file. It
records, as a separate and complete history, every state
that copy has passed through, together with a note on
each change saying what it was and why it was made. The
drawer of copies collapses back into one `analysis.R`,
and each copy becomes an entry in a history that can be
read, searched, and, if need be, restored.
The tool that has won this role, across the sciences and
across software of every kind, is git. The service that
most often hosts a git history on the network is GitHub,
with GitLab its principal institutional sibling. This
chapter teaches both from first principles. Version
control is the single most universally taught element of
a modern reproducibility course, and it is the
foundation on which the rest of this book stands.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: what the drawer loses

Of the three things the `FINAL`-file drawer loses, the
identity of the working version, the content of each
change, and the reason for each change, which one is
recoverable, laboriously, by reading the files
side by side, and which is not recoverable at all once
the analyst forgets or leaves?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

The content of a change, what differs between two
snapshot files, is recoverable by diffing them line by
line, though at real cost in effort. The reason for a
change is not recoverable from the files at all. It lived
only in the person who made the change, and once they
forget it or leave the project, it is gone for good.
Version control is useful precisely because the reason
is the one loss that no amount of careful reading of the
files themselves can undo.
:::
:::

It is also the foundation in a precise, technical
sense. The next chapter, @sec-compendium, makes the
compendium the unit of reproducible work, and
@sec-levels placed the bare compendium at the bottom
rung of the ladder, L0 locatable. The artifact that marks
L0 is exactly a version-controlled repository. That is, an analysis is
locatable when, and only when, it is under version
control and can therefore be found, read, and referred
to by a second person. Everything the later chapters add
is installed on top of a version-controlled history: the
lockfile of @sec-dependencies, the container of
@sec-containers, the continuous integration of
@sec-verification.

## The analyst's contribution

Version control automates the mechanics of history
perfectly and automates none of the judgment that
makes a history useful and safe. Three decisions belong
to the analyst and are the subject of this chapter as
much as the commands are.

1. **Deciding what must never be committed.** A commit
   is, by design, permanent and copied to every clone
   of the repository. The judgment of what may safely
   be made permanent and public, and what must be kept
   out of the history entirely, is the analyst's. In
   health research it is a judgment with legal and
   ethical force. Protected health information,
   identifiable data, and credentials must never enter
   the history. As we shall see, deleting them in a
   later commit does not remove them from it. This is
   the first and gravest of the three judgments.

2. **Choosing the granularity and the message of a
   commit.** A commit is a unit of change. How much
   change it should contain, and what its message
   should say, are matters of craft that no tool
   decides. A history of one enormous commit reading
   'did the analysis' is almost as useless as no
   history at all. A history of small, coherent commits
   whose messages say why each change was made is a
   readable record of decisions.

3. **Deciding when to branch and when to tag.** Whether
   a piece of work warrants a branch of its own, and
   whether a particular state of the analysis warrants a
   permanent tag, are design decisions about the shape of
   the history. They are cheap to make and expensive
   to omit. The state of the code at the moment a
   manuscript was submitted is worth a tag, and no tool
   will place it for the analyst.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: which judgment is health-specific

Of the three judgments listed above, which one carries
legal and ethical force specific to health research
rather than being craft judgment that applies to any
software project, and why?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

The first, deciding what must never be committed.
Choosing a commit's granularity and message, and
deciding when to branch or tag, are matters of craft
that apply to any software project, health-related or
not. The judgment that protected health information and
identifiable data must never enter the history carries
legal and ethical force specific to working with
human-subjects data. It is also the one judgment in this
chapter whose consequence, once realized, no git command
can undo.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## The vocabulary of this chapter

New terms are defined again on first use; they are
collected here for reference.

- **Repository (repo).** A directory whose contents
  and full history git tracks, held in a hidden
  `.git` subdirectory. A *clone* is a complete copy of
  a repository, history and all.
- **Working tree.** The ordinary files in the
  repository directory as they currently exist on
  disk, as opposed to the versions recorded in the
  history.
- **Commit.** A recorded snapshot of the tracked files
  at one moment, carrying an author, a timestamp, a
  message, and an immutable identifier (a *hash*). The
  atomic unit of history.
- **Staging area (index).** The set of changes marked,
  with `git add`, to go into the next commit. Staging
  lets a commit hold a chosen subset of the current
  changes.
- **`.gitignore`.** A file listing path patterns that
  git should not track, used to keep derived outputs,
  large data, and, above all, sensitive files out of
  the history.
- **Branch.** A movable name for a line of
  development. The default branch is conventionally
  called `main`, although git itself still names it
  `master` unless told otherwise, as with
  `git init -b main`.
- **Remote.** A copy of the repository hosted
  elsewhere, typically on GitHub or GitLab, used for
  backup, distribution, and collaboration. `origin` is
  the conventional name of the primary remote.
- **Tag.** A permanent, human-readable name for one
  specific commit, used to mark a milestone such as a
  manuscript submission.
- **Pull request (merge request).** A proposal, made on
  the remote, to merge one branch or fork into another,
  reviewed before it is accepted.
:::

## What version control records, and what it cures

The value of a version-control system is easiest to
state as the negation of the `FINAL`-file failure. That
failure loses three things, and version control
restores each.

It loses the *identity of the working version*. With a
drawer of dated copies, no file is authoritative. With
git, there is one `analysis.R`, and its history holds
every prior state, so the question 'which version is
current' cannot arise. It loses the *content of each
change*. Two snapshot files differ in ways that can be
recovered only by comparing them line by line by hand. A
git history presents each change as a *diff*, a precise
statement of the lines added and removed. Git computes
the diff on demand from the snapshots it stores, since
git keeps full snapshots, not diffs. Lastly, it loses the
*reason for each change*, the single most valuable and
most perishable piece of information about an analysis.
Why was the outlier-exclusion threshold changed from
three standard deviations to two? A dated file cannot say. A commit
whose message reads 'Tighten outlier threshold to 2 SD
per reviewer 2's comment' says exactly why, and the
record stays with the code.

The recorded reason is what makes version control an
instrument of scientific accountability. A
computational result is the end of a chain of
decisions, each of which could have gone otherwise. In a
regulated analysis, a clinical trial subject to audit, a
study destined for a guideline, the chain of decisions is
itself an object of scrutiny. 'Why did the estimate
change between the interim and the final analysis' is a
question an auditor is entitled to ask and the analyst is
obliged to answer. A commit history in which each change
carries its reason is most of the answer, already
written, dated, and attributed. It is, however, a record
of what the committers *asserted*, not a regulated audit
trail. The next section explains the difference.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: what one message restores

A commit message reads 'Tighten outlier threshold to 2
SD per reviewer 2's comment.' Which of the three things
the `FINAL`-file drawer lost does this message, by
itself, restore, and which two does it leave to the rest
of git's model?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

It restores the reason for the change, naming the
reviewer's request as the cause. It does not, by itself,
restore the identity of the working version, which comes
from git keeping one tracked `analysis.R` rather than a
drawer of copies. Nor does it restore the precise content
of the change, which comes from the diff the commit
carries alongside its message.
:::
:::

## The git model: repository, commit, history

Git is often taught as a list of commands to memorize,
which is why it is so often found bewildering. It is far
better understood as a small and coherent data model,
after which the commands follow naturally. There are
three ideas.

The first is the **repository**. A git repository is an
ordinary directory, the analyst's project, that git has
been told to track. Git then maintains, in a hidden
`.git` subdirectory, the complete history of everything
under that directory. The ordinary files the analyst
edits are the *working tree*; the `.git` directory is the
history.
Creating a repository is a single command run once in
the project directory.

```bash
cd diabetes-cohort
git init -b main
```

The `-b main` names the first branch `main`; without it,
git as of version 2.56 names it `master`, and the
`git push -u origin main` commands later in this chapter
would then fail. The git preflight of the setup appendix
([Git preflight](setup-appendix.qmd#sec-git-preflight)) sets `main` as the default once per
machine, together with the name and e-mail address every
commit records. It is worth running before this chapter's
first command.

The second idea, and the central one, is the **commit**.
A commit is a snapshot of the tracked files at one
moment, recorded together with four things: who made it,
when, a message describing it, and a hash that names it.
That hash is a forty-character SHA-1 string, usually
shown in an abbreviated form such as `a1b2c3d`. It is
computed over the whole commit object, and the snapshot
alone does not determine it. The commit object references
the snapshot, folds in the metadata, and records the hash
of the commit before it. (Git also supports repositories
that use the longer SHA-256 hash of sixty-four
characters, though SHA-1 remains the default.) Because
each commit's hash incorporates its parent's, the history
is a chain. No past entry can be altered without changing
its hash and the hash of every commit after it. The
hashes are, for practical purposes, unique, and git
guards against the known SHA-1 collision attacks with
built-in collision detection. The chain makes a history
*tamper-evident* in a narrow sense. Anyone who recorded a
commit's hash, in a tag, a manuscript, or a colleague's
clone, can detect that the history leading to it was
later changed.

But how much evidence is tamper-evidence? It is weaker
than it sounds, and anyone headed for regulated work
should know exactly how much weaker. The
author's name and e-mail address, and both dates a commit
carries, are whatever the committer's own git client
supplies. Setting `GIT_AUTHOR_DATE` and
`GIT_COMMITTER_DATE` and passing `--author` produces a
commit under another person's name dated years in the
past, which git accepts without complaint.

```bash
GIT_AUTHOR_DATE='2019-03-01T09:00:00' \
GIT_COMMITTER_DATE='2019-03-01T09:00:00' \
  git commit --author='Someone Else <someone@example.org>' \
    -m 'Backdated commit'
```

History is also rewritable by design. `git commit
--amend`, `git rebase`, and `git filter-repo` all replace
commits with new ones, and in a repository the analyst
controls nothing prevents it. The hash chain detects a
rewrite only for someone holding an earlier hash to
compare against. Assurance is added from outside the
commit. One source is commits signed with a key bound to
a verified identity. Another is a forge configured to
protect the main branch against force-pushes and to log
pushes, reviews, and merges on its own servers with its
own clock. Even then, a git history is not, by itself,
the audit trail that FDA's regulations require of
electronic records in the studies they cover. That trail
must be secure, computer-generated, and time-stamped, and must record
operator actions independently [@cfr21part11]. Within
those limits, a well-kept history is an honest and very
useful record of how an analysis was built. The rest of
this chapter treats it as that.

The third idea is the **history** itself, the chain of
commits, each pointing back to its parent, running from
the first commit to the most recent. Reading that chain
is reading the story of how the analysis came to its
current state. A branch, which we treat below, is
nothing more than a movable name pointing at one commit
in this structure.

The everyday cycle of work has just two steps against
this model. They exist because git deliberately separates
*choosing* what goes into a commit from *making* the
commit. First one *stages* the changes to be recorded,
with `git add`; then one *commits* the staged changes,
with `git commit`, attaching the message. The staging
step is not ceremony. It lets a single commit hold a
coherent subset of the work in progress, so that an
afternoon's editing across several concerns can be
recorded as several focused commits.

```bash
# edit analysis.R, then see what has changed
git status

# stage the file for the next commit
git add analysis.R

# record the staged change with a message
git commit -m "Add Cox model for 30-day readmission"
```

The message is the part of a commit that carries the
scientific value. The convention, which merits adoption
from the first day, is a short imperative summary line of
about fifty characters. It is optionally followed by a
blank line and a paragraph giving the *why*. 'Fix bug'
is a wasted message. 'Correct person-time denominator to
exclude pre-enrollment follow-up' is a message that will
still be intelligible, and still exculpatory, at an audit
three years later.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: why stage at all?

A colleague argues that the staging area is needless
friction: since one almost always wants to commit
everything one has changed, git should simply commit the
whole working tree and spare the analyst a `git add`.
What does the staging step buy that a commit-everything
model would lose?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

It buys the ability to make a commit an *atomic unit of
one idea* rather than a snapshot of whatever happened to
be on disk. In an afternoon an analyst may fix a bug in
the cleaning script, add an unrelated figure, and jot a
half-finished note in a third file. Committing all three
together produces a history entry that cannot be
described in one honest message and cannot be reverted
without disturbing unrelated work. Staging lets the
analyst record the bug fix as one commit, with its own
message and reason, and the figure as another, leaving
the unfinished note uncommitted. The history is only as
useful a record as its individual commits are coherent, and
staging is the mechanism that coherence requires. (For
the genuine everyday case where one *does* want
everything, `git commit -a` stages all tracked changes
in one step, so the friction is opt-out, not mandatory.)
:::
:::

## Reading the history: the log and the diff

Once a history exists, how do we read it? A history that
cannot be read is of little use, and git provides two
complementary views of it. The **log** is
the list of commits, most recent first, each with its
hash, author, date, and message. It is the table of
contents of the analysis's development.

```bash
# the full log
git log

# a compact one-line-per-commit view
git log --oneline

# which commits touched analysis/scripts/
git log --oneline -- analysis/scripts/
```

In a scratch copy of the worked example below, three commits
in, the compact view reads as follows. Each line is the
abbreviated hash and the summary line of the message, most
recent first.

```bash
# output abridged, from git 2.56.0
git log --oneline
#> c7d4711 Tighten outlier threshold to 2 SD per reviewer 2
#> a9aa55f Add cleaning script for registry extract
#> 936e050 Initialize compendium and .gitignore
```

The **diff** is the complementary view. Where the log
lists the changes, the diff gives the content of one.
`git diff` shows the changes in the working tree that
have not yet been staged. `git show` displays the full
diff of any single commit named by its hash, and
`git diff` between two commit hashes shows everything
that changed between them.

```bash
# what have I changed but not yet staged?
git diff

# show one commit's changes in full
git show a1b2c3d

# what changed between two points in the history?
git diff a1b2c3d f4e5d6c
```

Here is the diff from the same scratch repository, taken just
before the third commit, when one line of the cleaning script
had been edited. A line beginning `-` is the committed version
and a line beginning `+` is its replacement. The unmarked lines
are context, and the `@@` header gives their position.

```bash
# output abridged, from git 2.56.0
git diff
#> diff --git a/analysis/scripts/01-clean.R b/analysis/scripts/01-clean.R
#> --- a/analysis/scripts/01-clean.R
#> +++ b/analysis/scripts/01-clean.R
#> @@ -1,3 +1,3 @@
#>  cohort <- read.csv('analysis/data/raw_data/extract.csv')
#>  cohort <- subset(cohort, age >= 18)
#> -sd_cut <- 3
#> +sd_cut <- 2
```

Together the log and the diff answer the two questions
the `FINAL`-file drawer could not. The log tells us *when
and why* a thing changed, and the diff tells us *what
exactly* the change consisted of. To illustrate, consider
the commit history of the first weeks of an
incident-diabetes cohort study. It is rendered below as it
might appear to an auditor reviewing how the reported
hazard ratio came to be. The table is generated from
synthetic data, so that we may display a realistic
history without any real project's contents.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-audit-trail
#| tbl-cap: 'A synthetic commit history for the first weeks of a cohort analysis, read as a record of decisions. Each row is one atomic, message-bearing commit; together they record not only what changed but, in the message, why. Note the reviewer-driven change to the outlier threshold, the kind of decision an auditor is entitled to trace.'

library(tibble)
library(dplyr)
library(knitr)

commit_history <- tibble::tibble(
  hash = c('a1b2c3d', 'e4f5a6b', 'c7d8e9f',
           'b0a1c2d', 'd3e4f5a', 'f6a7b8c',
           'a9b0c1d'),
  date = as.Date(c('2026-02-03', '2026-02-05',
                   '2026-02-09', '2026-02-12',
                   '2026-02-18', '2026-02-24',
                   '2026-03-02')),
  author = c('analyst.a', 'analyst.a', 'analyst.a',
             'analyst.b', 'analyst.a', 'analyst.b',
             'analyst.a'),
  message = c(
    'Initialize compendium and .gitignore',
    'Add cleaning script for registry extract',
    'Build analysis-ready cohort table',
    'Fit Cox model for 30-day readmission',
    'Tighten outlier threshold to 2 SD per reviewer 2',
    'Add Kaplan-Meier figure to report',
    'Correct person-time denominator'),
  files_changed = c(2L, 1L, 3L, 1L, 1L, 2L, 1L)
)

commit_history |>
  dplyr::mutate(date = format(date, '%Y-%m-%d')) |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c('Hash', 'Date', 'Author',
                  'Message', 'Files'),
    align = c('l', 'l', 'l', 'l', 'r'))
```

Two features of this history could not come from a bare
list of files. The fifth commit records that the outlier
threshold changed *in response to a reviewer*. The final
commit records a correction to the person-time
denominator, the sort of methodological fix whose
provenance an auditor will want to establish.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: log or diff

An auditor asks two questions about @tbl-audit-trail:
'why did the outlier threshold change' and 'exactly which
lines changed when it did.' Which git view, the log or
the diff, answers each question?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

The log answers the first question: `git log` lists each
commit's message, and the fifth commit's message in
@tbl-audit-trail names the reviewer's request directly.
The diff answers the second: `git show` on that commit's
hash displays exactly which lines were added and removed.
Neither replaces the other; the log
without the diff says why but not what, and the diff
without the log says what but not why.
:::
:::

## What must never be committed: `.gitignore` and PHI

We come now to the gravest of the three judgments. A
commit records the files git is tracking, and by default
git offers to track every file in the working tree. Two
categories of file must be kept out of that net. The
mechanism for keeping them out is the `.gitignore` file,
a plain-text list of path patterns that git will refuse
to track.

The first category is the merely unwanted. These are
files that *can* be committed but *should not* be,
because they are regenerable or bulky and would only
clutter the history. Rendered outputs (a compiled PDF, an
`.html` report, the figures a script regenerates on every
run) are the clearest case. Committing them couples the
history to products that the code already determines.
Large raw data files bloat every clone. Editor and
operating-system cruft (`.Rhistory`, `.DS_Store`,
`.Rproj.user/`) is pure noise. None of these is
dangerous; all of them are better ignored.

The second category makes this section a matter of
ethics and law. It comprises files that must *never*
enter the history, because making them permanent and
shareable would be a breach. In health research three
kinds dominate.

- **Protected health information and identifiable
  data.** A file containing patient identifiers, dates
  of birth, medical-record numbers, free-text clinical
  notes, or any data from which an individual could be
  re-identified must never be committed. This is the
  first rule of version control in a health setting, and
  it admits no exception.
- **Credentials.** Database passwords, API tokens, the
  contents of a `.Renviron` holding a secret, private
  keys: a credential committed to a repository, and
  worse pushed to a remote, is a credential to be
  treated as compromised.
- **Restricted or embargoed data** more generally, under
  a data-use agreement that forbids redistribution, even
  when not directly identifying.

::: {.callout-important}
## Restricted data

Protected health information, identifiable data, and
anything held under a data-use agreement that forbids
redistribution must never go into a git history. The
rule admits no exception: not even briefly on a branch
that is never merged, and not even in a local repository
that will ever be pushed. A commit is permanent by
design and, once pushed, copied to every clone. The
gravest and least intuitive fact about git is that its
ordinary commands only ever *add* to the history. Suppose a file containing protected health
information is committed, and the mistake is noticed and
the file deleted in a later commit. The file is gone from
the working tree but *remains in full in the history*. It
is recoverable by anyone with a clone from the commit
that introduced it. The deletion is itself just another
commit layered on top; it conceals nothing. Removing the
file requires rewriting the history. That rewrite changes
every subsequent commit hash, cannot reach copies already
made, and is error-prone precisely when it matters most.
If the offending commit was ever pushed to a remote, one
must assume it has been cloned and cached beyond recall.
The only sound response is then to treat the exposed data
as disclosed and follow the applicable incident
procedure. The remedy is therefore prevention. That means
a correct `.gitignore` written *before* the first commit,
and the habit of reading `git status` before every commit
to confirm that nothing sensitive has been staged.
:::

When prevention has failed, the order of the response
matters more than the commands, and the commands are the
last step.

1. **Stop and report.** Push nothing further. If the
   commit reached any remote, a disclosure has occurred.
   Notify the data steward, privacy office, or IRB under
   the institution's incident procedure, because that
   obligation is not a technical question and does not
   wait for the cleanup.
2. **Rotate credentials first.** If the file held a
   password, token, or key, revoke or rotate it at once.
   A rotated secret is harmless wherever copies survive;
   a rewritten history is not a substitute
   [@githubsensitive].
3. **Rewrite the history on a fresh clone.** `git
   filter-repo` removes the file from every commit on
   every branch and tag. Its `--sensitive-data-removal`
   option also fetches all refs first and keeps the
   remote configured so that the result can be pushed.

   ```bash
   git clone https://github.com/lab/diabetes-cohort.git
   cd diabetes-cohort
   git filter-repo --sensitive-data-removal --invert-paths \
     --path analysis/data/raw_data/extract.csv
   # expect no output: the file is in no remaining commit
   git log --all --oneline -- analysis/data/raw_data/extract.csv
   git push --force --mirror origin
   ```

   The force-push may require branch protection to be
   lifted for the purpose and restored afterwards.

   ::: {.callout-warning}
   ## Regulated records

   In a repository that holds records under GxP or
   another regulated quality system, a history rewrite
   is a controlled change, not a cleanup. Before running
   it, open a deviation or incident, obtain QA approval
   under the organization's SOPs, document what is being
   removed and why, and keep whatever record of the
   pre-rewrite state the quality system requires. The
   audit-trail provision of 21 CFR Part 11 states that
   'Record changes shall not obscure previously recorded
   information' [@cfr21part11, sec. 11.10(e)]. A rewrite
   obscures that information by design, which is why the
   deviation record must carry what the history no longer
   does. Better still,
   keep regulated records out of a rewritable forge in
   the first place, so that the question never arises.
   :::

4. **Clean what the forge holds.** On GitHub the purged
   commits can remain reachable through cached views and
   pull-request references, which the owner cannot push
   over. Removing them requires a request to GitHub
   Support. Forks are not touched by the rewrite at all,
   and their owners must be asked to delete them
   [@githubsensitive].
5. **Replace every clone.** Every collaborator's clone
   still holds the file, and a collaborator who pulls and
   pushes from an old clone puts it back. Each one must
   delete the clone and clone afresh, and any copy outside
   the team's reach, a backup, a CI cache, a stranger's
   clone, is beyond recall [@githubsensitive].

In a scratch repository, a clone made before the rewrite
still lists the offending commit after the remote has
been cleaned; the rewrite reaches only the copies it is
run on and pushed to.

A `.gitignore` is a small file, and its content depends
on the archetype of the compendium, a classification the
next chapter, @sec-compendium, develops in full. For now
two archetypes suffice: a data-analysis compendium, whose
deliverable is a set of results from data, and an
R-package compendium, whose deliverable is reusable
code. The reproducibility machinery is identical
across archetypes; the list of files to ignore is not. A
**data-analysis compendium** ignores its *derived outputs
and its raw data*. These are the regenerable tables and
figures, and the large or sensitive registry extract that
must stay out of the history entirely. An **R-package
compendium** has no `analysis/` outputs to ignore but
must ignore its *build artifacts*. These are the
`.Rcheck` directory, the built `.tar.gz` and binary
archives, and the `src/` object files a compiled package
leaves behind. The two `.gitignore` files barely
overlap, and writing the right one is part of naming the
archetype.

```bash
# .gitignore for a data-analysis compendium
# --- sensitive: never commit ---
analysis/data/raw_data/*
.Renviron
*.pem

# --- regenerable outputs ---
analysis/figures/*
analysis/tables/*
analysis/report/*.pdf
analysis/report/*.html

# --- editor and OS cruft ---
.Rhistory
.RData
.Rproj.user/
.DS_Store
```

```bash
# .gitignore for an R-package compendium
# --- build artifacts ---
*.tar.gz
*.Rcheck/
src/*.o
src/*.so
# generated pkgdown site; a comment must be on its own
# line, since text after a pattern is part of the pattern
docs/

# --- editor and OS cruft ---
.Rhistory
.RData
.DS_Store
```

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Verification

A `.gitignore` that has never been watched blocking a
real file is untested. To see it hold, create a
file the pattern should catch and confirm git refuses it:
`touch analysis/data/raw_data/scratch.csv && git status`
should not offer to add the new file, because
`analysis/data/raw_data/*` already matches it. To make it
fail on purpose, comment out that one line in
`.gitignore`, repeat the `touch` and `git status`, and
confirm the file now appears as untracked and ready to be
staged. Then restore the line before doing anything else
(habit 4).
:::

Two refinements warrant mention. A leading `!`
re-includes a pattern otherwise ignored. This is how one
ignores a whole data directory but keeps a small,
non-sensitive example file or a data dictionary under
version control (`analysis/data/raw_data/*` followed by
`!analysis/data/raw_data/data_dictionary.csv`). Second,
a committed-by-accident file, once added to `.gitignore`,
is still tracked until explicitly untracked with `git rm
--cached`. Ignoring a file does not retroactively remove
an already-committed copy, which returns us to the
warning above.

This book's own repository applies the rule to its
running cohort. The extract
`analysis/data/raw_data/cohort_raw.csv` is synthetic and
describes no real person, yet it is not committed. What
is committed is the script that writes it,
`analysis/scripts/simulate_cohort.R`, which regenerates
the extract from stated parameters; a reader with a
fresh clone runs it once before the examples. The
`.gitignore` excludes the whole `raw_data` directory
rather than the one filename, so that a second extract
saved there under any name is excluded too. The check
below confirms that the generated extract carries
identifying-looking fields, that the generator is
present, and that the directory pattern is in force.

```{r}
raw <- load_cohort('../data/raw_data/cohort_raw.csv')
nrow(raw)
intersect(c('mrn', 'patient_name', 'dob'), names(raw))

gitignore <- readLines('../../.gitignore')
repo_state <- c(
  generator_present = file.exists('../scripts/simulate_cohort.R'),
  raw_dir_ignored = 'analysis/data/raw_data/*' %in% gitignore
)
repo_state
```

The generated extract carries
`r length(intersect(c('mrn', 'patient_name', 'dob'), names(raw)))`
of the three columns this section warns against, by name.
The synthetic
cohort invents an identifier, a name, and a date of birth
so that the risk appears in a real file instead of only in
prose. The generator is
`r if (repo_state[['generator_present']]) 'present' else 'missing'`,
and the pattern `analysis/data/raw_data/*` is
`r if (repo_state[['raw_dir_ignored']]) 'in' else 'absent from'`
the `.gitignore`, which is the arrangement a real project
should copy: the code that produces or fetches the extract
under version control, the extract itself never.

A `.gitignore` guards paths, however, and nothing else.
The tests in `inst/tinytest/` need a copy of the cohort,
and an earlier version of this repository met that need
by copying the extract to `inst/testdata/cohort_raw.csv`
and committing it. No ignore pattern covered that path, so
the identifier columns entered the history by a second
route while the first stayed closed. The fixture now at
that path is derived from the synthetic extract. It keeps
the rows and the duplicate structure the tests need, drops
the name and date-of-birth columns, and replaces each
record number with a pseudonymous `ID-0001`-style id.

```{r}
fixture <- load_cohort('../../inst/testdata/cohort_raw.csv')
intersect(c('mrn', 'patient_name', 'dob'), names(fixture))
all(grepl('^ID-[0-9]{4}$', fixture$mrn))
```

Replacing the file only added a commit, and the earlier
copy is still in the history. Two commands find it. The
first lists every commit, on any branch, that touched the
path; the second prints the header of the file as the
oldest of those commits recorded it.

```bash
git log --all --oneline -- inst/testdata/cohort_raw.csv
git show <oldest-hash>:inst/testdata/cohort_raw.csv | head -1
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
fixture_path <- 'inst/testdata/cohort_raw.csv'
git_lines <- function(...) {
  out <- tryCatch(
    suppressWarnings(system2('git', c('-C', '../..', ...),
                             stdout = TRUE, stderr = FALSE)),
    error = function(e) character(0)
  )
  if (is.null(attr(out, 'status'))) out else character(0)
}
git_ok <- nzchar(Sys.which('git')) && file.exists('../../.git')
fixture_log <- if (git_ok) {
  git_lines('log', '--all', '--format=%h', '--', fixture_path)
} else {
  character(0)
}
oldest_copy <- utils::tail(fixture_log, 1)
oldest_header <- if (length(oldest_copy) == 1) {
  utils::head(git_lines('show',
                        paste0(oldest_copy, ':', fixture_path)), 1)
} else {
  character(0)
}
old_copy_has_identifiers <- length(oldest_header) == 1 &&
  all(c('patient_name', 'dob') %in%
        strsplit(gsub('"', '', oldest_header), ',')[[1]])
old_copy_same_bytes <- length(oldest_copy) == 1 && identical(
  git_lines('rev-parse', paste0(oldest_copy, ':', fixture_path)),
  git_lines('hash-object', 'analysis/data/raw_data/cohort_raw.csv')
)
c(commits_touching_path = length(fixture_log),
  old_copy_has_identifiers = old_copy_has_identifiers,
  old_copy_same_bytes = old_copy_same_bytes)
```

`r if (old_copy_has_identifiers) paste0('Run on this repository when the page was rendered, the log listed ', length(fixture_log), if (length(fixture_log) == 1) ' commit' else ' commits', ' touching the path. The oldest, ', oldest_copy, ', still holds a copy whose header names patient_name and dob', if (old_copy_same_bytes) ', and its bytes are identical to the generated extract.' else '.') else if (!git_ok) 'The git history was not available when this page was rendered, so the check above could not inspect the earlier copy; the two commands show it on any clone.' else 'When this page was rendered, no commit touching the path held a copy with the identifier columns, so the earlier copy has been removed from this repository; it survives in any clone made before the removal.'`
Anyone holding a clone, made at any time since, can read
it. The data are synthetic, so nothing real has
leaked, but the pattern is the one by which real data
leak: an extract protected at one path and copied,
for a convenience such as a test, to another. Removing
the copy from the history would take the rewrite
described above, with every cost listed there; we keep it
as this worked example. Deriving the new fixture from the
extract is acceptable here only because the extract is
synthetic. Rows of real data with the name columns dropped
still carry dates, ages, and measurements that can
re-identify, so a fixture for a real project is generated
or built from the data dictionary, and a commit that adds
a data file under any path warrants the question of where
its rows came from.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: the same file, two archetypes

A `report.pdf` sits at the top of one analyst's ignore
list and is deliberately committed by another. A
`data_dictionary.csv` describing a restricted registry
is committed, while the registry extract it describes is
ignored. Explain both choices.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

The rendered `report.pdf` is a regenerable output. In a
data-analysis or manuscript compendium it is a product
the code reproduces on render, so committing it couples
the history to a derivative and is usually avoided. An
analyst who nonetheless commits it, perhaps to preserve
the exact submitted PDF as a fixed reference, is making a
defensible different judgment about what the artifact
is *for*. It is a judgment, not a rule.
The `data_dictionary.csv` and the registry extract sit on
opposite sides of the one line that is not a matter of
taste. The dictionary carries variable names and codings,
which are metadata and safe to share, and belongs in the
history so a reader can interpret the analysis. The
extract carries the protected health information itself
and must never be committed, whatever its convenience.
The `!` re-inclusion pattern exists precisely to keep the
safe metadata while ignoring the unsafe data beside it.
:::
:::

## Branches, lightly

With the history and its exclusions in place, we turn to
its shape. For a solo analyst working linearly, a single
line of commits on the `main` branch is often the whole
story, and it is honest to say so rather than to impose
ceremony. But two situations make branches worth the
small investment of learning them. The first is
*speculative work*: trying an alternative model
specification, or a reviewer's proposed reanalysis,
without disturbing the `main` line that produced the
current results. The second is *collaboration*, treated
in the next section. There each contributor works on a
branch of their own, and the branches are merged only
when ready.

A branch is created and switched to in one command, and
merged back with another.

```bash
# create and switch to a branch for a reanalysis
git switch -c sensitivity-analysis

# ... make commits on the branch ...

# return to main and merge the branch in
git switch main
git merge sensitivity-analysis
```

The mental model is the one given above: a branch is a
movable name for a line of development, and `main` is
merely the name given to the first branch, here by
`git init -b main`. Nothing about
branching changes the commit model; it only lets two
lines of commits coexist and later rejoin. We keep the
treatment light here. We shall return to the
collaborative use of branches, which is where they earn
their keep, when we reach pull requests.

@fig-branch draws the shape. The branch does not copy
the history. It names a new commit whose parent is a
commit on `main`, and the merge names a commit with two
parents. Everything before
the branch point is shared, and no hash anywhere in the
diagram changes when the branch is created or merged.

```{r}
#| label: fig-branch
#| fig-cap: 'A branch and its merge, drawn as the commit graph git actually stores. The lower line is `main`; the upper line is a sensitivity-analysis branch created at commit B and merged back at M. Commits A through C exist once and are shared by both lines: the branch adds commits rather than copying them. The merge commit M is the only commit in the diagram with two parents, which is what records that the two lines rejoined and when.'
#| fig-alt: 'A commit graph with two horizontal rows of circles joined by lines, with time running left to right. The lower row, labeled main, runs A, B, C, then the merge commit M, then D. The upper row, labeled a sensitivity-analysis branch, holds two commits S1 and S2. A line rises from B to S1, marking the branch point, and a line descends from S2 to M, the merge. M is annotated as the only commit with two parents. Commits A, B, and C lie on the shared portion of the graph rather than being copied onto the branch.'
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 2.5

library(ggplot2)
library(tibble)

nodes <- tibble(
  id    = c('A', 'B', 'C', 'M', 'D', 'S1', 'S2'),
  x     = c(1, 2, 3, 4.6, 5.7, 3.1, 4.0),
  y     = c(0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0.8, 0.8),
  shade = c(rep('main', 5), 'branch', 'branch')
)

edges <- tibble(
  x    = c(1, 2, 3, 4.6, 2, 3.1, 4.0),
  xend = c(2, 3, 4.6, 5.7, 3.1, 4.0, 4.6),
  y    = c(0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0.8, 0.8),
  yend = c(0, 0, 0, 0, 0.8, 0.8, 0)
)

ggplot() +
  geom_segment(data = edges,
               aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
               color = 'grey45', linewidth = 0.45) +
  geom_point(data = nodes, aes(x = x, y = y, fill = shade),
             shape = 21, size = 9, stroke = 0.5,
             color = 'grey30', show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(data = nodes, aes(x = x, y = y, label = id),
            size = 3, fontface = 'bold') +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(main = '#c3ddda',
                               branch = '#f0e2c4')) +
  annotate('text', x = 0.55, y = 0, label = 'main',
           hjust = 1, fontface = 'bold', size = 3.2) +
  annotate('text', x = 2.55, y = 0.8, label = 'branch',
           hjust = 1, fontface = 'bold', size = 3.2) +
  annotate('text', x = 4.6, y = -0.52,
           label = 'M: two parents', size = 2.9,
           color = 'grey25') +
  annotate('text', x = 2.0, y = -0.52,
           label = 'branch point', size = 2.9,
           color = 'grey25') +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-0.1, 6.1), ylim = c(-0.8, 1.1)) +
  theme_void()
```

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: what the merge changes

After creating and merging the `sensitivity-analysis`
branch of the example above, do any of the commit hashes
on `main` from before the branch was created change?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

No. A branch adds new commits whose parent chain points
backward to an existing commit on `main`; it never
rewrites or recopies what came before the branch point.
The merge adds one further commit with two parents rather
than replacing anything. Every hash that existed before
the branch was created, on `main` or anywhere else, is
exactly as it was. That is what @fig-branch's shared
commits A through C illustrate.
:::
:::

## Undoing things, and merge conflicts

Two kinds of trouble are common enough to deserve their
own section: a change that needs to be undone, and a
merge that git cannot finish by itself.

**Undoing.** Git has three distinct commands for undoing
work, and the right one depends on where the unwanted
change lives.

`git restore <file>` discards *unstaged* edits in the
working tree, putting the file back to its last committed
(or staged) content. It never touches history; there is no
commit to undo, only a draft to throw away.

```bash
# an edit no one has staged or committed
echo 'threshold <- 99' > analysis.R
git restore analysis.R
# analysis.R is back to its last committed content
```

`git reset` moves what `HEAD` points to. That is, it
moves the branch itself to an earlier (or different)
commit. The three flags differ only in how much else they
touch along the way:

- `--soft` moves `HEAD` and leaves everything else alone:
  the undone commit's changes reappear staged, ready to be
  recommitted differently.
- `--mixed`, the default, additionally unstages those
  changes, so they sit in the working tree, edited but not
  staged.
- `--hard` additionally overwrites the working tree,
  discarding the changes outright.

```bash
# move HEAD back one commit; --mixed is the default
git reset HEAD~1
# the undone commit's edits are now unstaged, not gone

git reset --hard HEAD~1
# the undone commit's edits are discarded entirely
```

A reset, like the `amend` and `rebase` discussed earlier
in this chapter, is a rewrite of what the branch name
points to, not an addition to history. The same caution
applies. A reset is harmless on commits that exist only
in the analyst's own clone. It is a serious act, needing
the collaborators' agreement and a force-push, once those
commits have been pushed or pulled elsewhere. A local
reset that moves past *commits* can usually be undone.
The discarded commits are not immediately deleted, and
`git reflog` lists where `HEAD` pointed before the reset,
so `git reset --hard <that-hash>` restores them. The
reflog records only commits, however. Edits that were
never committed are not in it, and `--hard` overwrites
them in the working tree. Unstaged edits are then gone
permanently; staged ones survive only as unnamed objects
that `git fsck --lost-found` can sometimes recover, file
by file and without their names. Before any
`--hard`, therefore, read `git status`, and commit or
`git stash` whatever uncommitted work should survive.

`git revert <commit>` takes the opposite approach. Instead
of moving `HEAD` backward, it makes a *new* commit whose
changes are the exact opposite of the one named, applied
on top of the current history. The reverted commit is left
untouched, in place, for anyone to read later. Because
revert only ever adds a commit, it is the one of the three
that is safe on a branch other people have already pulled;
reset and amend are not.

```bash
git revert HEAD
# creates a new commit, e.g. "Revert 'Add note line'",
# that undoes the previous commit's changes; the
# reverted commit itself still exists in the history
```

The choice can be stated briefly. For an edit that is not
yet staged, use `restore`. For a commit that exists only
on a private branch, `reset` is simplest. For a commit
that others may already have, use `revert` and let
history show both the mistake and its correction.

**Merge conflicts.** A merge like the one in @fig-branch
goes through cleanly whenever the two branches changed
different lines. When both branches change the *same*
lines of the *same* file, git has no way to choose between
them, and the merge stops partway, leaving the decision to
the analyst.

```bash
git switch main
git merge sensitivity-analysis
# Auto-merging analysis.R
# CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in analysis.R
# Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then
# commit the result.
```

`git status` reports the file as having 'unmerged paths',
and the file itself now contains both versions, separated
by conflict markers that git inserts directly into the
text:

```
<<<<<<< HEAD
threshold <- 4
=======
threshold <- 5
>>>>>>> sensitivity-analysis
```

Everything between `<<<<<<< HEAD` and the `=======`
divider is the current branch's version; everything
between the divider and the final marker is the version
being merged in. Resolving the conflict means editing the
file by hand down to the single version that should
survive. That may be one side, the other, or a
combination of both. The analyst then deletes the markers
themselves; nothing removes them automatically. Once the
file reads the way it should, the usual two-step cycle
finishes the merge. One runs `git add` on the resolved
file to tell git the conflict is settled, then
`git commit` to record the merge. (`git merge --abort`
backs out of the whole attempt instead, if the conflict
turns out to need more thought than a mid-merge edit
allows.)

```bash
# edit analysis.R to resolve the conflict, then:
git add analysis.R
git commit -m "Merge sensitivity-analysis: keep threshold 4"
```

A conflict is not git malfunctioning; it is git correctly
refusing to guess at a scientific decision, such as which
of two threshold values the analysis should use, that only
the analyst can make.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: which command for which undo

A collaborator has three problems: an edit in `analysis.R`
that was never staged and should be thrown away; a commit
made on a private branch, pushed nowhere, that turns out to
be wrong; and a commit on `main` that was already pulled by
two other collaborators and turns out to be wrong. Which
command fits each case?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

The unstaged edit: `git restore analysis.R`, since nothing
has been committed yet. The private, unpushed commit:
`git reset`, most simply `--hard` if the change should be
discarded outright, since no one else has a copy of that
commit to lose synchronization with. The already-shared
commit: `git revert`. Reset or amend would rewrite a
commit other clones already hold. Reverting instead adds
a new commit that undoes it without touching what
collaborators already pulled.
:::
:::

## The remote: GitHub, GitLab, and collaboration

Everything so far is *local*. The repository, its
history, and its branches all live in the `.git`
directory on one machine, and if that machine is lost, so
is the work. A **remote** is a copy of the repository
hosted elsewhere, on GitHub, on GitLab, or on an
institution's own server. Connecting a local repository
to a remote serves three distinct purposes that are worth
separating.

The first is **backup**. A remote holds a complete copy of
the history, so that a lost laptop costs at most the
commits made since the last push. The second is
**distribution**. A public remote is the mechanism by
which a compendium becomes locatable to the world. It is
a URL a reviewer can be given, a repository a reader can
clone, the concrete form of the L0 rung of the ladder. The third
is **collaboration**, the purpose that shapes the rest of
this section.

The commands that connect to and synchronize with a
remote are few. One names the remote once, then pushes
local commits to it and pulls others' commits from it.

```bash
# connect the local repo to a remote named origin
git remote add origin https://github.com/lab/diabetes-cohort.git

# push the main branch and remember the link
git push -u origin main

# later: send new local commits up
git push

# and bring collaborators' commits down
git pull
```

Consider a team working across sites, a clinical trial
with several participating centers, a multi-institution
consortium. Such a team works in one of two models on
GitHub and GitLab. In the **shared-repository** model,
every contributor has write access to one repository,
works on a branch of it, and the `main` branch is
protected so that nothing reaches it without review. This
is the usual arrangement for a private trial repository,
where forking is often disabled. In the
**fork-and-pull-request** model, a contributor without
write access *forks* the canonical repository, making a
personal copy on the remote, and works on a branch of
that fork. In either model the contributor opens a **pull
request** (GitLab calls it a *merge request*, the same
thing under another name) proposing that the branch be
merged into `main`. The pull request is a unit of review.
The maintainers see exactly the diff being proposed,
discuss it inline, request changes, and merge it only
when satisfied. In a multi-site analysis, the pull
request is a documented, attributable, reviewable gate
through which every change to the shared analysis passes.
Its record, who proposed what, who reviewed it, what was
said, and when it was merged, is held on the forge's
servers rather than asserted by a client. It therefore
complements the commit history with a record of the
*review* of each change that is harder to backdate. That
record is review evidence, not by itself a regulated
signature. An approval on a forge does not, by default,
carry the printed name, the date and time, and the
meaning of the signature that 21 CFR 11.50(a) requires
of a signed electronic record [@cfr21part11]. Whether it
counts as a controlled approval depends on the
organization's validated configuration of the forge and
on its SOPs.

The same gate serves when the contributor is a coding agent.
The agent works on a branch of its own and opens a pull
request; the analyst reads the diff, reviews it, and alone
decides whether to merge. The agent's account of its change
is a description to check against the diff, not a substitute
for reading it (@sec-llm-delegate).

The last piece of the remote's vocabulary is the pair
**tags and releases**, and they matter to reproducibility
specifically. A tag is a permanent, human-readable name
for one commit. `git tag -a v1.0-submission -m "State at
journal submission"` marks, forever and unambiguously, the
exact state of the analysis at the moment a manuscript was
submitted. A *release* on GitHub or GitLab is a tag dressed
with notes and downloadable archives. The reproducibility
payoff is that a reviewer, or the analyst a year later,
can recover the precise state that produced the submitted
numbers by naming the tag. There is no need to guess
which commit was current on the submission date. In
@sec-archiving we shall see the same tagged state
deposited to a public archive with a citable identifier.
The tag is the local anchor to which that archival
identity attaches.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: what does the pull request add?

A single analyst, working alone, keeps a clean commit
history with careful messages. A reviewer asks why, if the
history already records each decision, a multi-site trial
should bother with the additional machinery of forks and
pull requests. What does the pull request record that the
commit history does not?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

The commit history records what changed and, in its
messages, why. It does not record who *reviewed* the
change before it entered the shared analysis, or what
they said. In a solo project there is no reviewer, so
nothing is lost. In a multi-site trial, a change to the
shared analysis by one center affects every center's
results. There the review is itself a controlled step,
and the pull request is the artifact that records it: the
proposed diff, the discussion, the requested changes, the
approval, and the merge, each attributable and
timestamped. The commit
history answers 'what was changed and why'; the pull
request answers 'who checked it, and did they agree'. For a
regulated analysis both questions have auditors.
:::
:::

## What git does not do

Having made version control the foundation, we must be
exact about the boundary of what it provides. The whole
discipline of this book is matching a claim to what has
actually been secured. Git versions *text and tracks its
history*. It records every state of the files under it
and the reason each committer gave for each change. That
is the entirety of what it does, and it is the L0 rung of
the ladder. An analysis under version control is
locatable, findable and readable by a second person, and
no more.

In particular, git does not pin the *package versions* an
analysis uses. A repository cloned a year later contains
the same `analysis.R`, but running it installs whatever
package versions are current. These may not be the
versions the analyst used, so the code that ran may no
longer run, or may run and return a different number. Git
also does not pin the *computational environment*. The R
version, the operating system, the system libraries a
package links against are nowhere in the history, and a
clone is at the mercy of whatever the next machine
provides. These are exactly the layers of the determinant
stack that @sec-levels enumerated as unpinned at L0.
Closing them is the work of the two chapters that follow.
The lockfile of @sec-dependencies pins the package layer
to reach L1, and the container of @sec-containers pins the
environment layer to reach L2. Version control is
necessary for all of this, since the lockfile and the
Dockerfile are themselves files whose history git tracks.
It is sufficient for none of it.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: history without a lockfile

A repository has a full, well-written commit history, a
tag marking the submitted manuscript, and is hosted on
GitHub. Has it reached L1?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

No. Everything described pins the analysis code and makes
it locatable, which is exactly L0. Reaching L1 requires a
lockfile recording the exact version of every package the
analysis used, and no amount of git history, however
complete, records that on its own. A repository can be a
model of version-control discipline and still sit at L0 if
no lockfile exists.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## The honest level

This chapter's own practice reaches L0, locatable, by
placing the repository under version control and pushing
it to a remote. The cohort extract is not part of that
history; its generator is, and the extract is regenerated
from it. The practice leaves every layer beneath the
analysis code, the packages, the environment, and the
rest of the determinant stack, exposed and unpinned.
:::

## Worked example

To make the chapter concrete, we take the
incident-diabetes cohort of the running example from an
untracked folder to a tagged, remotely hosted repository.
We stay at the level of the commands and the judgment
behind them. The shell sessions below are not executed when
the book renders. The outputs shown with `#>` were captured
once, on 2026-11-08, from a scratch copy of the example with a
synthetic identity, and are abridged.

The analyst begins with a folder of scripts and a registry
extract. The very first act, before a single commit, is to
write the `.gitignore`, because the extract contains
protected health information that must never enter the
history.

```bash
cd diabetes-cohort
git init -b main
# write .gitignore FIRST, ignoring raw_data and credentials
git status --untracked-files=all   # is the extract listed?
```

The flag matters. Plain `git status` collapses a directory
that holds no tracked files into one line, here `analysis/`,
so it cannot show whether the extract inside is ignored.
Run on a scratch copy of this example, the full listing names
the extract before the `.gitignore` is written and omits it
after, and `git check-ignore -v` names the rule responsible.

```bash
# output abridged, from git 2.56.0
# before .gitignore
git status --untracked-files=all
#> Untracked files:
#>   DESCRIPTION
#>   analysis/data/raw_data/extract.csv
#>   analysis/scripts/01-clean.R

# after .gitignore
git status --untracked-files=all
#> Untracked files:
#>   .gitignore
#>   DESCRIPTION
#>   analysis/scripts/01-clean.R

git check-ignore -v analysis/data/raw_data/extract.csv
#> .gitignore:1:analysis/data/raw_data/  analysis/data/raw_data/extract.csv
```

Only once `git status` confirms that the sensitive extract
is ignored does the analyst make the first commit, the one
that lifts the folder to L0, locatable. Its output names the
branch, marks the commit as the root of the history, and
lists the files it records.

```bash
git add .gitignore DESCRIPTION
git commit -m "Initialize compendium and .gitignore"
# output abridged, from git 2.56.0
#> [main (root-commit) 936e050] Initialize compendium and .gitignore
#>  2 files changed, 4 insertions(+)
#>  create mode 100644 .gitignore
#>  create mode 100644 DESCRIPTION
```

A commit that stops instead with 'Please tell me who you are'
means git has no identity on this machine. The
[Git preflight](setup-appendix.qmd#sec-git-preflight) sets it, and
[When git refuses](setup-appendix.qmd#sec-git-refuses) lists this and
the other refusals a first push can meet.

Work proceeds as a sequence of small, message-bearing
commits: the cleaning script, the derived cohort table,
the Cox model. Each is its own commit with its own reason,
exactly the history tabulated in @tbl-audit-trail. When a reviewer
later asks why the outlier threshold changed, the answer is
one `git log` away.

To try a reviewer's proposed reanalysis without disturbing
the results already reported, the analyst branches.

```bash
git switch -c reviewer-sensitivity
# ... reanalysis commits ...
git switch main            # main is untouched and still runs
```

The work is backed up and made locatable by connecting a
remote and pushing.

```bash
git remote add origin https://github.com/lab/diabetes-cohort.git
git push -u origin main
# output abridged, from git 2.56.0 (local stand-in remote)
#>  * [new branch]      main -> main
#> branch 'main' set up to track 'origin/main'.
git status
#> On branch main
#> Your branch is up to date with 'origin/main'.
```

The last line of the push is the one to look for: the local
`main` now tracks the remote's, so a later bare `git push` or
`git pull` knows where to go. The scratch run pushed to a
local bare repository rather than to a forge, so its output
omits the forge's own progress lines. A push that is refused
instead is diagnosed from [When git refuses](setup-appendix.qmd#sec-git-refuses).

A collaborator at a second site forks the repository, adds
a site-specific adjustment on a branch of their fork, and
opens a pull request. The analyst reviews the diff inline,
requests one change, and merges it, leaving a reviewable
record of the exchange. Finally, at journal submission, the
analyst marks the exact state.

```bash
git tag -a v1.0-submission -m "State at journal submission"
git push origin v1.0-submission
```

The folder is now a version-controlled, remotely hosted,
tagged repository. It is firmly at L0, with a clean
history, a reviewed collaboration record, and a permanent
anchor to the submitted state. It is *not* yet L1 or L2,
because nothing has pinned the packages or the
environment, and the honest reproducibility statement
says exactly that. The
lockfile of @sec-dependencies is the next commit.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: what the worked example still lacks

At the point the worked example ends, tagged, pushed, and
with a reviewed pull request merged, what single artifact
would need to be added for the compendium to reach L1, and
is adding it itself a version-control operation?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

A lockfile, such as `renv.lock`, recording the exact
version of every package the analysis uses. Writing it is
not a version-control operation in the sense this chapter
teaches; it belongs to @sec-dependencies. Version control
will track the lockfile once it exists, exactly as it
tracks any other file, but producing it is a different act
from committing, branching, or tagging.
:::
:::

## Collaborating with an LLM

A language model is a fluent assistant for git, which is
a domain rich in memorized command recipes. Precisely
that fluency is the hazard. Check every command it proposes
for operations beyond what was asked, irreversible ones
above all; the model does not know which of the analyst's
files are sensitive. A coding
agent that works in the repository can read those files,
run git itself, and push. It is therefore run only in
projects whose data it is allowed to see, and never with
credentials that let it push to a remote unreviewed.

{{< include _llm-rule.qmd >}}

For git, the structure a prompt describes is the
repository's: its paths and file types, not the contents
of the files. The three triples below mark the division of
labor.

**Prompt.** 'I accidentally committed a file of patient
data three commits ago. Give me the git commands to remove
it.'

*Watch for.* A history-rewriting recipe (`git filter-repo`,
or the older `filter-branch`, or a `reset`) presented as a
clean fix. The model cannot know whether the offending
commit was ever pushed to a remote. That is the fact that
determines whether removal is even possible, so check
whether the answer raises the breach question at all.

*Verification.* Treat the exposure, not the git command, as
the primary problem. Establish first whether the commit was
pushed. If it was, assume the data has been cloned and
cached and follow your institution's incident procedure,
because no git command can recall it. Only then apply a
rewriting tool, on a fresh clone and in the order the
five-step procedure earlier in this chapter gives, and in
a repository of regulated records only as the approved,
documented change its third step requires. Check that the
recipe covers the forge's caches, forks, and every
collaborator's clone. A coding agent asked the same question
does not stop at a recipe: it can run the rewrite and the
force-push itself. The breach assessment, the decision to
rewrite, and the force-push stay with the analyst. At most
the agent prepares the commands on a fresh clone, for the
analyst to read and run (@sec-llm-delegate).

**Prompt.** 'Write a `.gitignore` for my R health-data
analysis project.'

*Watch for.* A generic R `.gitignore` (the standard
`.Rhistory`, `.RData`, `.Rproj.user/` list) that omits the
one category that matters most, the raw data and
credentials specific to *your own* project. A chat model
has not seen your directory. A coding
agent may have listed it, but a file's name does not say
whether it holds PHI. An agent that opened the files to
find out has already read the data, which is why it
belongs only in projects it is cleared to see.

*Verification.* Take the generic list as a starting point,
then add, by hand, the explicit paths of every raw-data
directory, every `.Renviron` or credential file, and every
restricted dataset. Confirm with `git status` that each is
untracked before the first commit. The generic patterns
are safe to accept; the project-specific sensitive paths are
yours to supply.

*A better prompt.* 'Below is the directory tree of my R
analysis compendium, file names only, with no file opened.
Write a `.gitignore` that excludes `analysis/data/raw_data/`,
`.Renviron` and any other credential file, and regenerable
outputs, but keeps the code, `renv.lock`, and the synthetic
cohort tracked. Label each line generic or project-specific,
and list the commands that would show me each sensitive path
is ignored.'

**Prompt.** 'Write good commit messages for these changes.'

*Watch for.* Messages that fluently describe *what*
changed, which the model can read from the diff, but
invent or omit the *why*. The why is the scientifically
load-bearing part, and the model cannot know it. A
plausible-sounding 'Update outlier threshold' hides the
reviewer request that the record must carry.

*Verification.* Supply the reason yourself. Let the model
draft the imperative summary line from the diff, then edit
in the motivation, the reviewer comment, the corrected
denominator, the protocol amendment, that turns a
description into an accountable record.

## Exercises

1. Take a folder of your own currently versioned by the
   `FINAL`-file method, count the manual snapshot files it
   contains, and for two of them state what changed between
   them and why. Note which of those two questions you can
   still answer, and use the difficulty as a measure of what
   a commit history would have preserved.

2. Initialize a git repository in a scratch directory, make
   three commits that each change one file, and then use
   `git log --oneline` and `git show` to recover, for the
   middle commit, both what changed and the message you
   wrote. Confirm that the commit hashes are unchanged by a
   later commit.

3. Write a `.gitignore` for a data-analysis compendium and a
   second for an R-package compendium, and list the patterns
   that appear in one but not the other. Explain each
   difference in terms of what the archetype produces.

4. Explain, to a colleague who has just deleted a
   PHI-containing file in a new commit and believes the
   problem solved, why the file is still in the history, what
   determines whether it can be removed, and what to do if
   the offending commit was already pushed to GitHub.

5. Construct the sequence of commands by which a collaborator
   at a second trial site would contribute a change through a
   fork and a pull request, and state, for each step, what
   part of the project's record it adds that a direct push to
   `main` would not.

6. An analyst pushes a version-controlled compendium to
   GitHub and writes in the methods section that the analysis
   is 'fully reproducible'. State the rung the analysis has
   actually reached, name the two layers of the determinant
   stack that remain unpinned, and rewrite the sentence so
   that it claims exactly what version control secures and no
   more.

7. In a fresh clone of this book's repository, run
   `Rscript analysis/scripts/simulate_cohort.R` from the
   top directory, then
   `raw <- load_cohort('analysis/data/raw_data/cohort_raw.csv')`.
   Report `nrow(raw)` and the three columns among
   `names(raw)` that would, in a real project, require the
   extract to sit behind the `.gitignore` pattern
   `analysis/data/raw_data/*`, and use
   `git check-ignore -v analysis/data/raw_data/cohort_raw.csv`
   to name the line that excludes it. Then run
   `git log --all --oneline -- inst/testdata/cohort_raw.csv`
   and state what the oldest commit it lists shows about
   whether that pattern kept the identifier columns out of
   the history.

8. This exercise returns to the determinant stack and the
   L0-to-L3 ladder of Chapter 3 (@sec-levels). A colleague
   deletes the `.git` directory of a well-tested, fully
   containerized analysis and runs `git init` again to
   'start clean' before pushing, so the repository now
   hosted on GitHub shows a single commit from yesterday.
   Using what this chapter and @sec-levels together
   establish, state the rung the repository occupies
   today, and explain what the colleague's own prior
   discipline, the lockfile and the container, can and
   cannot restore of what the deleted history held.

## Solutions

Attempt an exercise before expanding its solution. The first
two ask you to work in your own directories, so what you
produce will vary; the boxes say what a good answer
establishes.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 1

No single correct answer. What a good answer establishes is
the asymmetry between the two questions, because the
asymmetry is the argument for version control.

Almost every reader can answer *what changed* between two
snapshot files, because the files are still there and a
diff tool will show it. Almost no reader can answer *why*,
because the reason was never written down anywhere. It
lived in the analyst's head, or in an email, or in a
conversation after a meeting, and it is gone. Readers
commonly find they can reconstruct the what for files a
year old and cannot reconstruct the why for files a month
old.

That gap is precisely what a commit history preserves.
The diff is recoverable from the files themselves, so it
is the cheaper half; the message is not recoverable from
anything, so it is the half that decays. This is why the
chapter insists that a commit is an atomic unit of one
idea with a message attached. The message is the only part
of the record that cannot be reconstructed later.

If you find that you *can* answer why, because you named
the files carefully, you have demonstrated the `FINAL`
method working at its best. Notice, then, how much of
the reasoning fits in a filename.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 2

The mechanics are straightforward, so the substance is the
last clause.

```bash
git init
# edit file_a.txt
git add file_a.txt && git commit -m 'Add the cohort filter'
# edit file_b.txt
git add file_b.txt && git commit -m 'Raise the outlier threshold'
# edit file_c.txt
git add file_c.txt && git commit -m 'Add the summary table'
git log --oneline
git show <middle-hash>
```

`git log --oneline` lists the three commits newest first,
each with an abbreviated hash and its subject line.
`git show` on the middle hash prints both halves of the
record: the message you wrote, and the diff of what
changed.

On the hashes: recording the middle commit's hash before
making the third commit and comparing afterward shows it
unchanged. A commit hash is
computed over the commit's content *and* its parent's
hash, so it fixes the entire history leading to it. Adding
a commit on top cannot alter it, because the new commit
points backward and nothing points forward. That is the
property that makes the history tamper-evident to anyone
who recorded a hash.

The honest qualification, which a careful reader may
raise: hashes are stable under *adding* history, not under
*rewriting* it. An `amend` or a `rebase` produces new
commits with new hashes, and the old ones become
unreferenced. A rewrite is detectable only by someone who
kept an old hash, and the author and dates inside each
commit were set by the committer's own client in the first
place. The record is trustworthy for a history that is
appended to and whose hashes are held elsewhere, in tags,
in collaborators' clones, on a protected forge. That is
why rewriting shared history is treated as a serious act.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 3

Your own files will differ in detail. Taking the two
samples in this chapter as the model answer, they barely
overlap, and the difference follows from what each
archetype produces.

Common to both: the editor and operating-system cruft,
`.Rhistory`, `.RData`, and `.DS_Store`.

In the **data-analysis** file but not the package one: the
raw-data extract, `analysis/data/raw_data/*`, which carries
the protected information; the regenerable outputs,
`analysis/figures/*`, `analysis/tables/*`, and the rendered
