`*.pdf` and `*.html` reports, since the report is a product
the code regenerates; and `.Renviron`, `*.pem`, and
`.Rproj.user/`.

In the **R-package** file but not the analysis one: the
build artifacts, `*.tar.gz` and `*.Rcheck/`; the compiled
object files `src/*.o` and `src/*.so`, which exist only if
the package carries compiled code and are rebuilt on every
install; and `docs/`, the generated pkgdown site.

The last three analysis-only lines are differences of the
abridged samples, not of the archetypes. Credentials and
editor state can appear in any project, so a package
repository should ignore `.Renviron`, `*.pem`, and
`.Rproj.user/` as well. A good answer says so.

The explanation to give for each remaining difference has
the same shape. An archetype ignores what it *generates*
and commits what it *is*. A data-analysis compendium
generates a report and so ignores it. A package generates
a tarball, check output, compiled objects, and a website,
and so ignores those. Neither ignores its own source.

The one line that is not a matter of archetype is the data
carrying protected health information. It is ignored in
every archetype, always, and is the subject of the next
exercise.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 4

The colleague's mental model is that a repository holds the
current state of the files. It holds their whole history,
and that is the point of it.

**Why the file is still there.** Deleting a file in a new
commit records the deletion as a change. The commit that
added the file is untouched, and the file's contents are
retrievable from it by anyone who clones the repository.
The deletion is a new fact appended to the record, not an
erasure of the old one.

**What determines whether it can be removed.** Whether the
history has been shared. Removing content means rewriting
every commit from the offending one forward, with
`git filter-repo` or an equivalent, which produces new
hashes for all of them. If the offending commit exists only
in the local repository, this is a local operation and
costs nothing but care. If it has been pushed, every clone
and fork holds the old objects, and rewriting the local
copy does not touch them.

**What to do if it was already pushed to GitHub.** Treat
the data as disclosed and act in that order. Notify whoever
is responsible for the data, an IRB or a privacy office,
because a disclosure has occurred and the notification
obligation is not a technical question. Rotate anything
rotatable. Then rewrite the history and force-push, and
ask GitHub Support to purge cached views and any dangling
objects. Require every collaborator to re-clone rather
than pull, since a pull onto a rewritten history
reintroduces the old objects. Note the ordering: the
cleanup is the last step and the least important one,
because it does not undo the exposure.

This is why the `.gitignore` for protected data is written
before the first commit rather than after the first
mistake.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 5

A serviceable sequence, with what each step adds to the
record.

```bash
# 1. Fork the canonical repository on the forge.
git clone https://github.com/<site2>/<study>.git
cd <study>
git remote add upstream https://github.com/<coord>/<study>.git

# 2. Branch from an up-to-date main.
git fetch upstream
git switch -c fix/outlier-threshold upstream/main

# 3. Commit the change.
git add R/clean_cohort.R
git commit -m 'Raise outlier threshold to 4 SD per SAP amendment 2'

# 4. Push to the fork and open a pull request.
git push origin fix/outlier-threshold
```

What each step records that a direct push would not. The
**fork** lets a contributor without write access to the
canonical analysis propose a change, which then cannot
enter without someone else's action. (A fork does not show
that the contributor lacked write access; anyone may fork.
On a private trial repository with forking disabled, a
branch of the shared repository with a protected `main`
plays the same role.) The **branch**
separates the proposal from the accepted state, so the
history of `main` contains only what was agreed. The
**commit** is the same in either workflow and records what
and why. The **pull request** is the artifact that carries
everything a direct push destroys. It holds the proposed
diff before it was accepted, the discussion, any requested
changes and the revisions answering them, the identity of
the approver, and the timestamp of the approval. The
**merge** records that the approval preceded the entry
into `main`.

The compressed version of the answer: the commit history
answers 'what changed and why'; the pull request answers
'who checked it, and did they agree'. A direct push to
`main` answers only the first, and in a multi-site trial
the second question has auditors too. In a regulated
trial, the approval is review evidence rather than, by
itself, an electronic signature under 21 CFR 11.50(a);
whether it serves as one depends on the sponsor's
validated configuration and SOPs. The analysis change
behind the commit is itself approved through the
sponsor's own process, here an amendment to the
statistical analysis plan, not through the pull request.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 6

**The rung reached is L0.** Version control makes the
analysis locatable and gives it a history. It pins the
analysis code, which is a real achievement and the
precondition for everything above it. However, the ladder
grades how far *down* the determinant stack a result is
locked, and the code sits at the top of that stack.

**Two layers that remain unpinned.** The first is the
package versions, since nothing in a git repository
records which version of `dplyr` produced the numbers. The
second is the environment beneath them, the R runtime,
the operating system, and the system libraries. You may
equally name the numerical libraries or the session
configuration and be right, since the repository touches
neither. The common wrong answer is to name the data,
which version control *can* pin for a small committed
dataset, though usually does not for a large or protected
one.

**A rewritten sentence.** 'The analysis code is version
controlled and deposited at [location], so the exact code
that produced these results can be retrieved. The software
environment was not recorded; re-execution may therefore
require package versions differing from those used here,
and we have not verified that the results regenerate.'

The three clauses map onto the three claims: what is
secured, what is not, and what has not been checked. The
last clause is the one authors most often omit, and it is
the difference between claiming L0 honestly and claiming
L3 by implication.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 7

The solution for this exercise is in the
[Instructor Guide](instructor-guide.qmd#sec-ig-vc),
which is available to course instructors. Self-study
readers who want to check their answer can compare it
with the executed output of the cohort checks in the
`.gitignore` section of this chapter: the row count and
identifier columns of the generated extract, the
directory pattern, and the history of
`inst/testdata/cohort_raw.csv`. The point of the last
step is that `git check-ignore` succeeds on the extract
while the oldest copy of the fixture, on the render of
this page,
`r if (old_copy_has_identifiers) 'still carries' else 'could not be shown to carry'`
the identifier columns: the pattern held at its own path,
and the copy entered the history by another.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 8

**The rung is L2, unchanged by the deletion.** The
repository that is hosted on GitHub today is still
locatable, so L0 holds and a reviewer can find and read
it. This is so even though its visible history begins
with yesterday's single commit. Nothing about `git init`
run fresh touches the lockfile or the container. Those
files, if they still sit in the working tree, are tracked
again by the new history and hold the analysis at L1 and
L2 exactly as before. Package pinning and environment
pinning are properties of *files*, not of the commit chain
that records them. If the analysis had reached L3, its
baseline test is a file too and survives, but the CI
runs that showed it passing were attached to commits that
no longer exist. L3 is reached only by verification, so it
must be shown again by a fresh run of that test after a
clean rebuild.

**What is lost, and what is not.** The lockfile and the
container restore the analysis's position on the capture
ladder, L1 and L2. `renv.lock` and the Dockerfile are
ordinary files that a fresh `git init` tracks exactly as
well as the old history did. What they cannot restore is
the history itself: the sequence of decisions, the
reviewer-driven changes, the dated and attributed record
@tbl-audit-trail exemplifies, and any tag that marked a
past submission. That record is not a determinant of the
computational result at all, so no rung of the L0 to L3
ladder grades its loss. It is a loss of scientific
provenance and accountability, which is this chapter's
subject rather than the ladder's. What the colleague
erased is the one part of the record a baseline test or a
container rebuild was never designed to protect.
:::

## Cheat sheet {#sec-cheat-vc}

| Command or rule | What it does |
|---|---|
| `git init -b main` | Starts tracking the current directory as a repository, with the first branch named `main`. |
| `git add <file>` | Stages a change for the next commit. |
| `git commit -m '...'` | Records the staged changes with a message. |
| `git status` | Shows staged, unstaged, and untracked files; read it before every commit (habit 3). |
| `git log --oneline` | Lists commits, most recent first, by hash and message. |
| `git show <hash>` | Displays one commit's full diff. |
| `git switch -c <name>` | Creates and switches to a new branch. |
| `git remote add origin <url>`; `git push -u origin main` | Connects to, and first pushes to, a remote. |
| `git tag -a v1.0 -m '...'` | Marks one commit permanently, e.g. at submission (@sec-archiving anchors to this). |
| `!pattern` in `.gitignore` | Re-includes a path otherwise ignored, e.g. a data dictionary beside an ignored extract. |
| `git check-ignore -v <path>` | Names the `.gitignore` rule that ignores a path, or prints nothing if none does. |
| `git rm --cached <file>` | Untracks a file already committed; does not erase it from the history. |
| Git refuses | Look up the message in [When git refuses](setup-appendix.qmd#sec-git-refuses); run the [Git preflight](setup-appendix.qmd#sec-git-preflight) once per machine. |
| `git filter-repo --sensitive-data-removal` | Rewrites every commit to remove a file; only on a fresh clone, only before re-pushing. Where records are regulated, only as an approved, documented controlled change. |
| Rule of thumb | PHI, credentials, and restricted data are never committed; deleting them later does not remove them from the history. |
| Rule of thumb | Version control reaches L0 only; it pins the analysis code, not the packages or the environment. |
| Habit 1 | Commit before you compute. |

## Further reading

- @ram2013 is the direct argument for git as an instrument
  of reproducibility and transparency in science. It is the
  natural first reading for a researcher who has met git
  only as a software tool, and it makes the case for the
  commit history as a record of scientific provenance.
- @bryan2018 is the standard orientation to version control
  written for data scientists rather than software
  engineers. It motivates GitHub as the collaboration
  substrate with the working analyst's concerns foremost.
  The longer online book by Bryan and colleagues, *Happy
  Git and GitHub for the useR* [@bryanhappygit], is the
  companion practical manual. The setup appendix points to
  its chapters on installing git, identity, and
  credentials.
- @wilson2017 and @sandve2013 place version control among
  the good practices of reproducible computational
  research. The former treats it as one of a set of habits
  for scientific computing, and the latter places it among
  its rules for reproducible analysis. Read them to see
  version control situated alongside the other pillars
  this book develops.
- The layers that version control does not pin are the
  subject of @sec-dependencies and @sec-containers. The
  continuous integration and collaboration built upon a git
  history are developed in @sec-verification and in
  @sec-archiving; this chapter is best read as the
  foundation those four presuppose.
